summary:
Vladimir Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and no regional deviation from that framework has been identified. For a visitor the national law applies in full: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Any police, hotel or transport identity check therefore reads a mismatch that cannot be corrected.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' law is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising 6-10 years under Article 282.2. Foreign visitors who violate these provisions face arrest, detention and deportation, and official national government warnings to LGBT travellers say so explicitly.

Enforcement is documented and ongoing. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols; between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state being able but not willing to provide protection.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Physical coercion against transgender people is also documented: BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two preceding years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
localsOnly:
For residents of Vladimir Oblast the national regime operates as a permanent legal condition rather than a border risk: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are prohibited outright, gender markers on documents cannot be changed, and same-sex marriage is unavailable. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

The Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, and that the state is able but not willing to provide protection. Records at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports Vladimir Oblast-specific enforcement data: the extremism convictions, administrative cases and propaganda-law fines are recorded at national level, so the local application of those figures in Vladimir Oblast is unresolved. Whether oblast-level police or courts have diverged from the national pattern in either direction is not sourced here.

The claim that no regional deviation has been identified rests on the absence of contrary reporting rather than on an affirmative regional survey, and should be read as unresolved rather than confirmed. The current status of the conversion-therapy facility reported near Novosibirsk, and whether comparable private coercion facilities operate in Vladimir Oblast, is not sourced.
